chapter: Chicago, Villa Venice and Louis Armstrong
title: Petrillo's threat and the Villa Venice show
summary: On opening night Petrillo threatens to run the Black band off, Budd describes the grand Villa Venice with gondolas, and how they transposed foreign acts' music.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: That was a high class joint, but I

will never forget when Petrillo called out there on opening night and said if you don't get them niggers off that job in thirty minutes I'm going to send out my gangsters, and we're going to run them off the job. So this guy -- this was Albert Boucher's Villa Venice, and he called us all --
That's right, Papa Boucher. It was a place on 32 acres, and they had gondolas and everything, nothing but rich people come out there.
This out -- I'm glad, I want you to explain this place, how it looked, Budd. Explain it.

Oh, it was a dream. They had lights and all, like Christmas lights, and everything, all in the trees. They had gondolas where here come this boss out with his secretary. He could get on the boat like you're in Venice, and the cat would sing to you and row you to your little house where you could have sexual intercourse with the girl, and they come back into the club, and they had like the King Sisters there. They had like all of these foreign people with their shows, and they would bring in their music, and we would -- I had to translate -- transpose everything, I mean like clarinet in C, and clarinet in E flat, and I only had one clarinet, B flat, and clarinet in E, and oboe parts, and everything, you know.
Like we -- we weren't playing all those instruments,
but we were able to transpose --
Transpose, because you were good musicians.
And then, you know, because we had gone through the school of hard knocks, and all the expense we had, so this is why the guy called us in.
